title: Picking a Crypto Library — When and Why

questions.question: What does AEAD give you that “just encrypt with AES” does not?
options: Confidentiality + integrity/authenticity in one primitive
Faster encryption by removing the need for a key
A guarantee that the code is constant-time in all languages
The ability to recover the plaintext without knowing the nonce
questions.explanation: AEAD modes (e.g., AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) provide authenticated encryption: they protect both confidentiality and integrity.

questions.question: In Python, what is the best default when comparing a server-computed tag (MAC) to attacker-provided bytes?
options: `hmac.compare_digest(expected, provided)`
`expected == provided`
`expected.hex() == provided.hex()`
`expected.startswith(provided)`
questions.explanation: `compare_digest` is designed to avoid content-based short-circuiting and is the right default for verifying tags.

questions.question: Which library/API characteristic most strongly suggests a misuse-resistant approach to encryption?
options: It provides high-level AEAD APIs (encrypt+authenticate) as the primary “happy path”
It exposes many cipher modes and lets the user pick from a long list
It focuses on being minimal and avoids documentation to reduce mistakes
It supports encryption but does not mention integrity or authentication
questions.explanation: Misuse-resistant libraries tend to make the safe construction (AEAD) the default path, instead of pushing users into mode/padding choices.

questions.question: Why is “the library was audited” not a complete argument by itself?
options: Audits have a limited scope and time window; you still need maintenance, adoption, and safe APIs
Audits guarantee the library will never have bugs again
Audits are only useful for proprietary libraries, not open source
Audits make performance irrelevant because security is solved
questions.explanation: An audit is evidence, not a permanent guarantee. You still need active maintenance, secure defaults, and a safe API surface.

questions.question: For this course, what is the best default choice for SHA-256 and HMAC-SHA-256 in Python?
options: Use stdlib `hashlib` for hashes and stdlib `hmac` for HMAC
Use a third-party crypto library for all hashing and MAC operations
Implement SHA-256 and HMAC yourself in production code for control
Use base64 strings for inputs so you avoid dealing with bytes
questions.explanation: The stdlib provides stable, widely deployed implementations for common hashes and HMAC. Third-party libraries are still needed for things like AEAD.

questions.question: Which practice best reduces supply-chain risk when using crypto dependencies?
options: Pin versions, keep dependencies minimal, and review changes when upgrading
Always upgrade to the newest version immediately without reading release notes
Prefer the library with the most GitHub stars, regardless of releases
Copy-paste a single file from a repository to avoid package managers
questions.explanation: Supply-chain hygiene is about controlling what you install and when. Pin versions, upgrade deliberately, and keep the dependency set small.

questions.question: If you need AEAD encryption in a production Python service, which is the safest direction?
options: Prefer a high-level AEAD API (e.g., `cryptography`'s `AESGCM` / `ChaCha20Poly1305`)
Prefer raw AES mode selection so you can choose ECB for simplicity
Prefer encrypt-then-encode without authentication because it “looks random”
Prefer designing a custom mode so your ciphertexts are unique to your app
questions.explanation: High-level AEAD APIs reduce foot-guns by bundling encryption + authentication correctly and avoiding manual mode/padding decisions.

questions.question: What is the core risk of a library that primarily exposes low-level primitives (raw RSA, manual padding, many AES modes) as its main entry points?
options: It makes it easy to build something that works on happy paths but is insecure under adversarial input
It makes cryptography impossible because low-level primitives never work
It guarantees constant-time behavior by avoiding high-level helpers
It prevents interoperability because low-level primitives are non-standard
questions.explanation: Low-level APIs can be correct but are easy to misuse. Misuse-resistant APIs aim to make the safe construction the easiest path.
